claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure comprising phase distributions and microstructural features at multiple length scales.
Image-derived and statistical descriptors can quantitatively represent the hierarchical heterostructure.
A machine-learning-augmented multiscale model can correlate local phase interfaces and grain-boundary distributions with tensile and fracture responses.
The morphology and phase distribution of the hierarchical heterostructure mediate localized stress and strain partitioning.
Localized stress and strain partitioning affect the overall mechanical response of HfNbTiVAl10.
Capturing microstructural inhomogeneities allows local stiffness variations and stress-concentration sites to be related more directly to macroscopic mechanical properties.
Machine learning can refine the mapping between microstructural descriptors and measured deformation parameters.
The proposed framework can bypass some computational cost and uncertainty associated with conventional finite-element or ab initio simulations.
The proposed model will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior more accurately than traditional simulation methods.
The proposed model will reduce prediction error for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness by approximately 10–20% relative to conventional simulations.
The proposed model will reduce computational time by approximately 30% relative to conventional simulations.
Nonuniform presence of the heterostructural features may cause the approach to fail.
Microstructural variability outside the machine-learning training range may cause the approach to fail.
Extreme temperatures or loading rates may induce microstructural evolution absent from the initial descriptors and thereby cause the approach to fail.
The comparison will use independently measured Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness as reference outcomes.

The hypothesis is falsified unless the augmented model achieves at least a 10% error reduction and approximately 30% or greater computational-time reduction relative to conventional methods across a majority of samples.
